questions.question: A geologist drops a quartz crystal into a big, empty glass jar. Quartz is a solid. What does every solid have, whatever container holds it?
questions.answer: Its own shape and its own volume
choices: Its own shape and its own volume
Its own volume, but not its own shape
Its own shape, but not its own volume
Neither its own shape nor its own volume
questions.context: A solid such as quartz keeps its own shape and its own volume, so it looks the same in a box or a jar. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container, and a gas has neither: it spreads out to fill whatever holds it.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.8.1 compares solids, liquids and gases, and its lessons teach that a solid keeps its shape and volume in a new container.

questions.question: A diver swims through the sea, breathing air from a tank. Seawater is a liquid, and air is a gas. What is one difference between them?
questions.answer: Only the seawater keeps its own volume
choices: Only the seawater keeps its own volume
Only the air keeps its own volume
Only the seawater keeps its own shape
Only the air keeps its own shape
questions.context: A litre of seawater still takes up one litre, poured into a jug or a bucket. A gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it, and it can be squeezed into a small space, as the air in a diver's tank is. Neither one keeps a shape of its own: both take the shape of their container.
questions.grade_note: Grade 5 lessons for Florida's SC.5.P.8.1 teach that a liquid changes shape but not volume in a new container, while a gas expands to fill its container.

questions.question: A runner breathes out on a chilly autumn morning, and a white puff hangs in the air in front of his face. What is the white puff made of?
choices: Tiny drops of liquid water
Tiny crystals of solid ice
Water vapour from his lungs
Warm air from his lungs
questions.context: Water vapour, the gas form of water, cannot be seen. When warm, damp breath meets cold air, some of its water vapour condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, and the drops make the white puff. A fog of ice crystals usually needs far colder air, around -35 degrees Celsius or below.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 matter lessons teach that water vapour is invisible and that the steam that can be seen is droplets of liquid water.

questions.question: A student packs a beaker with crushed ice and a little cold water, then stands a thermometer in it. What does the thermometer read while the ice slowly melts?
choices: 0 degrees Celsius
32 degrees Celsius
10 degrees Celsius
-10 degrees Celsius
questions.context: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, and water freezes at the same temperature. While ice and water are mixed, the heat that flows in goes into melting the ice, so the mixture stays at about 0 degrees until the ice is gone. On the Fahrenheit scale that temperature is 32 degrees.
questions.grade_note: Measuring the temperature at which water changes state, in degrees Celsius, is taught by grade 5 (England's Year 4 states of matter), and 0 degrees Celsius for melting ice is the basic number.

questions.question: In a lab beside the sea, a scientist heats a beaker of pure water until it boils hard. What temperature does her thermometer show while the water boils?
choices: 100 degrees Celsius
212 degrees Celsius
80 degrees Celsius
150 degrees Celsius
questions.context: At sea level, pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, or 212 degrees Fahrenheit. Once it boils, more heat turns more water into vapour but does not make it any hotter. High on a mountain, where the air pressure is lower, water boils below 100 degrees.
questions.grade_note: Water boiling at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level is one of the two temperatures every 5th grader learns for water's changes of state, alongside 0 degrees for freezing.

questions.question: A scientist rests a lump of the silvery metal gallium in her palm, and the solid metal slowly turns into a shiny liquid. What makes it turn to liquid?
questions.answer: Heat flowing into it from her hand
choices: Heat flowing into it from her hand
Cold flowing out of it into her hand
Sweat from her hand dissolving it
Air around it reacting with it
questions.context: Heat flows from her warm hand into the cooler metal, and a solid that takes in enough heat melts. Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, cooler than human skin, while ice melts at 0 degrees and iron only at about 1,538. Neither sweat nor air turns it liquid, and cold never flows at all: only heat moves, from warmer things to cooler ones.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.9.1 teaches that adding heat causes changes of state, and 'cold flows from one object to another' is a known grades 3-5 misconception (Ohio State).

questions.question: Lava pours from a volcano, glowing at over 1,000 degrees Celsius. As it cools, the liquid rock hardens into solid black rock. Which change of state is this?
choices: Freezing
Melting
Condensation
Evaporation
questions.context: Freezing is any liquid turning into a solid as it loses heat. Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, but melted rock freezes while it is still hundreds of degrees hot, so lava hardening into rock such as basalt is freezing too. Melting is the opposite change, solid to liquid.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders learn freezing as a liquid turning solid when heat is taken away (Florida SC.5.P.9.1); lava is the unit's rock example of that same change.

questions.question: A scientist screws the lid onto a glass jar full of ice cubes. Soon tiny drops of water cover the outside of the jar. Where does the water come from?
questions.answer: Water vapour in the air around it
choices: Water vapour in the air around it
Melted ice seeping through the glass
Cold leaking out and turning to water
Water vapour from the ice inside it
questions.context: Air holds water vapour, an invisible gas. When the air touches the cold glass it cools, and some of its water vapour condenses into drops of liquid water on the outside of the jar. The lid is shut tight and glass lets no water through, so none of the drops comes from inside the jar.
questions.grade_note: Condensation on a cold container is the standard grade 5 example of cooling causing a change of state, and 'water comes through the glass' is a documented belief at ages 8 to 15 (Osborne and Cosgrove).

questions.question: Water boils hard in a glass beaker over a lab burner, and big bubbles rise all through it and burst at the top. What is inside the big bubbles?
questions.answer: Water in the form of a gas
choices: Water in the form of a gas
Air that was mixed in the water
Heat from the burner's flame
Oxygen and hydrogen split from water
questions.context: The big bubbles are water vapour, water turned into a gas, so boiling makes no new substance; cooled again, the vapour condenses back into liquid water. The tiny bubbles that appear as water first warms are different: they are air that was dissolved in it.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.9.1 teaches boiling as heat turning water into a gas, and the air, heat and oxygen-and-hydrogen ideas about the bubbles are documented from age 8 (Osborne and Cosgrove).

d9c399335b.why: Judge (low, clarity): 'Only a liquid keeps its own volume' was true only within the pair, and a child who knows a solid keeps its volume too could balk at 'only'. The choices now name the two substances of the stem ('Only the seawater...', 'Only the air...'), so 'only' is scoped to the pair. Same key fact (F3, F4); stem and context unchanged.

85d0ce30af.why: Fact-check (uncertain) and judge (low): 'Ice crystals form instead only in far colder air, at about -35 degrees Celsius or below' was firmer than the sources ('generally' at or below -35, F8). The last sentence now reads 'A fog of ice crystals usually needs far colder air, around -35 degrees Celsius or below.' Stem, choices and key unchanged.

be8600b1fe.why: Judge (medium, grade): naming solid-to-liquid 'melting' is grade 2-3 content and the stem's 'warmth of her hand' and 'solid into liquid' left one live choice; it also shared its four choices with the lava question. Re-keyed, as the judge proposed, to what makes it melt: heat flowing in from her hand (F14, F15). The lures are real confusions: cold flowing out (Ohio State's 'cold is transferred', F23), sweat dissolving it (dissolving taken for melting), and the air reacting with it; gallium does not react with water or air at room temperature (F24). The stem no longer names the warmth.

75288e1e47.why: Judge (medium): the key was the only choice in the unit's science words, and 'The glass sweating, as skin does' was near-dead. Replaced that lure with 'Water vapour from the ice inside it', so two choices say water vapour and the screwed-on lid becomes the clue the child must use. The context now says glass lets no water through (F25, Grokipedia Glass, checked now); its last sentence on heat and freezing was cut to make room. Stem and key unchanged.
